extracted.intended_audience: clinical chemical analysts / medical laboratory technicians performing quantitative urine analyses
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural laboratory protocols and interpretive guidance for quantitative assays on urine (urea, total nitrogen, chloride, pigments) including reagent recipes, apparatus, step-by-step operations, corrections and calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypobromite reagent concentration warning
rubrics_metrics.description: La décomposition de l’urée étant plus complète avec un réactif riche en alcali. Il ne faudrait pas cependant préparer une solution hypobromique dépassant notablement ce degré de concentration ; car on s’exposerait ainsi à la voir dégager de l’oxygène.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a hypobromite reagent sufficiently alkaline for complete urea decomposition but avoid preparing it too concentrated to prevent oxygen evolution (hazard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypobromite reagent recipes for urea assay
rubrics_metrics.description: Two formulations given for hypobromite used in urea determination: (a) lessive de soude non carbonatée (densité 1.33) 60 c.c., eau distillée bouillie 60 c.c., bromé 5 c.c.; or (b) soude caustique fondue 24 gr., eau distillée bouillie 110 c.c., bromé 5 c.c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare one of the two indicated formulations and follow subsequent procedural timing and dilution instructions for reproducible urea decomposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ureometer handling and timing for urea assay
rubrics_metrics.description: After reaction, leave apparatus on the mercury trough 8–10 minutes to allow reaction completion; then transport ureometer into a test-tube of water at lab temperature (or immerse for 4–5 minutes up to the tap) before raising to read gas volume; avoid holding apparatus at the analyst's level to prevent warming the gas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strictly follow the described waiting times and handling to ensure complete reaction and accurate gas-volume measurement; avoid warming the collected gas when reading volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of standard titrated urea solution and repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: After measuring nitrogen volume from urine, immediately repeat the operation under same conditions using a titrated urea solution in proportion so it gives sensibly the same nitrogen volume; the urea test sample should be supplemented with the same quantity of glucose and reacted with the same volume of hypobromite; maintain constant laboratory and water-bath temperatures between runs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform paired measurements (urine and standard) under identical conditions (reagents, glucose presence, temperature) to allow direct comparison and calculation of urea content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction for non-urea nitrogen (ammoniacal salts and creatinine)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treatment of urine with lead subacetate does not remove creatinine nor ammoniacal salts; these release nitrogen with hypobromite and increase measured nitrogen above that from urea alone. Unable to precisely evaluate ammoniacal nitrogen, it is left counted as urea. For creatinine, assume creatinine nitrogen is 2% of urea nitrogen and that creatinine yields about 50% of its nitrogen under the hypobromite conditions; therefore subtract 1% of the measured nitrogen volume as due to creatinine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the stated approximate corrections: do not attempt to remove ammoniacal nitrogen (accepted 1–2% possible contribution), subtract 1% of measured N for creatinine contribution when estimating urea from hypobromite measurements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calculation of urea from measured nitrogen volumes
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the corrected nitrogen volume from urine with that obtained from the titrated urea solution to determine corresponding amount of urea in the 2 cc urine sample; then calculate urea in 24-hour urine if needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the paired measurement and corrections to compute urea mass per test volume and scale to 24-hour excretion when applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of method for total nitrogen: Dumas vs Kjeldahl
rubrics_metrics.description: Dumas combustion yields most exact results for total nitrogen but is lengthy and difficult; Kjeldahl method (with small modifications) gives very satisfactory results and is preferred for routine determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer Kjeldahl for routine total nitrogen assays unless Dumas apparatus and time are available and required for highest precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kjeldahl first step — conversion of organic nitrogen to ammonia
rubrics_metrics.description: Transform nitrogen of organic matter into ammonia by heating sample with concentrated sulfuric acid; ammonia fixed as sulfate may then be displaced by base and separated by distillation or decomposed by hypobromite (Henninger modification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carry out sulfuric acid digestion carefully to remove water and carbonaceous material; follow recommended additions and heating until liquid is dark/black then clarified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and addition of oxidants during digestion (permanganate/manganese dioxide)
rubrics_metrics.description: Permanganate of potash (or manganese dioxide) can be added in small portions to hasten combustion, but must be added cautiously to avoid violent reaction. However, Henninger recommends avoiding these oxidants when later measuring ammonia with hypobromite because manganese compounds form brown precipitates that hinder nitrogen release and reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If subsequent hypobromite/ureometer measurement will be used prefer to digest with sulfuric acid alone (longer time) to avoid Mn oxide interference; if using permanganate add it in very small portions and with safety precautions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neutralization/saturation and preparation of digest for ammonia determination
rubrics_metrics.description: After digestion and cooling, add 0.20–0.30 centigrams permanganate (if used), heat until liquid clears, cool, add 2–3 drops of tournesol tincture (indicator), then add decarbonated lye (NaOH) dropwise with agitation until turbidity appears but stop before color turns fully blue; decant into a 50 cc volumetric flask, wash, and make up to 50 cc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neutralize/saturate cautiously to avoid overshooting; return slight precipitate by adding 1–2 drops sulfuric acid if necessary to restore clarity before decanting and bring to exact volume for reproducible subsampling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distillation apparatus and dimensions for ammonia distillation
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternate to Schloesing apparatus: use a matras/balloon 125–150 cc (preferably long neck) connected to an abduction tube with approximate dimensions a-b 32–35 cm, b-c 16–18 cm, internal diameter at least 6 mm; attach a Will and Warrentrapp nitrogen tube inverted; bulb capacities g,h at least 30 cc; matras placed on Bunsen with wire gauze; receiving tube to be immersed in water trough.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct apparatus respecting the given dimensions and sturdy connections (especially the wide end of the Will & Warrentrapp tube) to obtain distillation results comparable to commercial apparatus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for ammonia distillation and titration
rubrics_metrics.description: Place 10 cc titrated sulfuric acid plus 2–3 drops tournesol in the receiving bulbs, connect and immerse in water; measure 10 cc of ammoniacal liquid (equiv. to 2 cc urine) into matras, add 85 cc distilled water, pumice, and 5 cc decarbonated NaOH (excess), heat to moderate boiling and maintain until about half the liquid has distilled into the receiving bulbs (approx. 40 minutes). Separate receiving bulbs from condenser before stopping heat to avoid absorption. Transfer receiver contents to a saturation flask and titrate excess sulfuric acid with standardized NaOH; difference P gives acid neutralized by ammonia. Convert to ammonia weight and then to nitrogen using provided stoichiometric equations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the exact volumes, heating/collection technique (detach receiver before extinguishing heat) and perform titration calculations per the given formulae to obtain accurate nitrogen content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Henninger modification for faster Kjeldahl (ammonia measured by hypobromite)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of distilling ammonia into titrated acid, decompose the ammonia in the aliquot by sodium hypobromite and volumetrically measure the nitrogen in a ureometer. For this, avoid oxidants during digestion (permanganate etc.) because Mn salts form precipitates that hinder nitrogen evolution; digest with sulfuric acid alone until decoloration (often 1–1.5 hours), bring final liquor to 50 cc, take 10 cc (2 cc urine) and react with hypobromite + glucose in ureometer, note volume V and repeat with titrated ammonium sulfate to get V'; use provided equations to compute ammonia/total nitrogen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Henninger modification for speed but ensure digestion without oxidant adjuvants and carefully match conditions between sample and standard runs for correct volumetric comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject certain catalytic adjuvants during digestion
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjuvants previously used to accelerate organic transformation (sulfate/oxide of copper, metallic mercury and its oxide, perchlorate and bichromate of potash, bichloride of platinum, etc.) must in all cases be absolutely rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use these adjuvants because they interfere with subsequent determinations or introduce contaminants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calculation of total nitrogen and azoturic ratio (R)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute total nitrogen in the 2 cc urine aliquot from titration results (equations provided: relate P to x etc.), compute nitrogen due to urea (z) from urea assay, and then compute azoturic ratio R = z / y (ureic N divided by total N).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the stated stoichiometric conversion factors and algebraic relations exactly as shown to derive weights of ammonia, nitrogen, urea and the final ratio R.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolation and identification of urobiline pigment
rubrics_metrics.description: If present in notable amount, isolate urobiline by acidifying 100 cc filtered urine with 2–3 drops H2SO4, saturate with ammonium sulfate, shake, rest 1–2 hours, filter, wash deposit with saturated ammonium sulfate slightly acidified, press filter, digest at 40–50°C with alcohol ~0° slightly ammoniacal; evaporate the alcohol to recover urobiline. Characterization: add trace ammonia and ZnCl2 to produce fluorescent dichroic liquid (rose by reflection, green by transmission) and spectroscopic band near F line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the precipitation, washing, gentle digestion and spectral/fluorescence checks to confirm urobiline identity; alternate rapid method by adding conc. fumigating HCl, heating, extracting with ether which gives green fluorescence in ether extract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clinical interpretation ranges for urinary sodium chloride
rubrics_metrics.description: Sodium chloride is the most abundant mineral in urine (about two-thirds of mineral weight). Normal 24-hour urinary NaCl ~10–12 g. In simple polyuria and especially diabetic polyuria it may rise substantially (up to or above 30 g/day). Large decreases occur in intense febrile illnesses (pneumonia) and total absence of NaCl in urine may indicate imminent death (Méhu).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the given expected ranges to inform clinical interpretation: increases often indicate improving state when originally low; decreases in acute disease indicate severity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volumetric (Mohr) method for chloride (NaCl) determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Dose chloride by precipitating chlorine as AgCl using standardized silver nitrate in presence of potassium/sodium chromate as indicator: prepare residue from 10 cc urine (neutralize with NaOH, add KNO3, evaporate to dryness, heat to clarity), dissolve in warm water, neutralize with nitric acid and add excess powdered calcium carbonate (left in excess), add 3–4 drops saturated neutral potassium chromate, then titrate with standardized AgNO3 until a persistent reddish coloration appears. Conversion: 1/100th cent. cub. division = 0.0106068 g chlorine = 1 mg NaCl in the 10 cc aliquot; multiply by 100 for g/L.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform evaporations, neutralizations and titrations exactly as described; constant and indicator addition ensure end-point detection; apply given conversion factor for final result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gravimetric method for chloride determination
rubrics_metrics.description: From calcination residue of 10 cc urine (prepared as above), dissolve, render acid with nitric acid, add slight excess AgNO3, allow precipitation and stand, decant and filter; wash AgCl until washings are not clouded by HCl; dry precipitate and incinerate on filter (or suspend in flame on platinum wire) then treat residue with regia to convert reduced silver back to AgCl, evaporate to dryness, incinerate again until AgCl nearly fuses at edges; cool in desiccator, weigh; subtract filter ash and convert AgCl weight to chlorine by factor 0.2474 and to NaCl by factor 0.4076.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow thorough washing, controlled incineration, and conversion of reduced Ag to AgCl with regia to ensure accurate gravimetric result; apply conversion factors to get chlorine/NaCl weights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rapid volumetric chloride method for routine clinical use
rubrics_metrics.description: Expeditious method (Pribram, Denigès): for routine clinical monitoring, partially burn organic matter in urine with permanganate (10 cc urine + equal volume permanganate 200‰), then titrate directly with standard silver solution. Method yields sufficiently accurate results for lightly colored and not overly dense urines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this quicker method only for routine follow-up, and restrict to urine samples that are not very colored and have density not greatly above normal to avoid interferences; it's faster but less universally applicable than full methods.
